subject: paediatrics
title: Pediatric Ocular Malignancies: Retinoblastoma and Leukocoria

steps.tx: Malignant transformation of primitive neuroepithelial retinal photoreceptor precursor cells represents the commonest primary intraocular malignancy of childhood. Characteristically diagnosed within the first two years of life, **pediatric retinoblastoma** arises from homozygous inactivation of the RB1 tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 13q14. The tumor may be unilateral and sporadic, or bilateral and heritable, threatening vision and life.
steps.say: Retinoblastoma is the most common intraocular cancer of childhood, caused by RB1 mutations on chromosome 13. It can be sporadic and unilateral, or heritable and bilateral.

vis.alt: Clinical eye photograph displaying leukocoria (white pupillary reflex) and cross section showing intraocular calcified retinoblastoma.
vis.caption: White pupillary reflex (leukocoria or cat's-eye reflex) characteristic of pediatric retinoblastoma. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: The pathognomonic physical finding noticed by parents or detected on red reflex screening is white pupillary discoloration. Clinically termed the cat's-eye reflex, **leukocoria in retinoblastoma** accounts for sixty percent of initial clinical presentations, where a chalky-white, vascularized intraocular mass replaces the normal red fundal reflex. The second most frequent presenting manifestation is strabismus (squint), resulting from macular involvement disrupting visual fixation.
steps.say: Leukocoria, or a white pupillary reflex, is the commonest presentation of retinoblastoma. Strabismus is the second most common sign, caused by macular tumor involvement.

left.title: Classic Presenting Signs
points: Leukocoria (white pupillary reflex in 60% of cases)
Strabismus (esotropia or exotropia in 20% of cases)
Painful red eye with secondary neovascular glaucoma
Pseudohypopyon from anterior chamber tumor seeding

right.title: Red Reflex Screening (Bruckner Test)
points: Examine pupils in darkened room with direct ophthalmoscope
Normal: symmetrical, bright, orange-red fundal reflex
Abnormal: dull, white, yellow, or asymmetrical reflex
Mandates urgent specialist pediatric ophthalmology referral

steps.tx: Differential diagnostic evaluation of a white pupillary reflex encompasses several benign and congenital ocular conditions in childhood. While retinoblastoma represents the most urgent life-threatening diagnosis, **differential diagnosis of leukocoria** includes congenital cataracts, persistent fetal vasculature (persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous), retinopathy of prematurity, Coats disease with retinal telangiectasia, toxocariasis, and retinal astrocytoma.
steps.say: The differential diagnosis of leukocoria includes congenital cataract, Coats disease, persistent fetal vasculature, and toxocariasis. Retinoblastoma must be ruled out urgently.

rows: Opacity of the crystalline ocular lens
Unilateral in young boys (6-8 yrs), yellow lipid
Failure of primary vitreous hyaloid regression

steps.tx: Knudson two-hit hypothesis elegantly explains the genetic and clinical divergence between heritable and non-heritable retinoblastoma. In **heritable bilateral retinoblastoma** (forty percent of cases), the first mutation is inherited via germline cells (present in all body cells), requiring only a single somatic mutational hit in retinal cells, resulting in early bilateral, multifocal tumors and an elevated lifetime risk of secondary malignancies like osteosarcoma.
steps.say: Under Knudson two-hit hypothesis, heritable retinoblastoma involves a germline mutation plus a somatic hit, causing early bilateral tumors and high risks of osteosarcoma.

left.title: Heritable Retinoblastoma (40%)
points: Germline RB1 mutation (chromosome 13q14)
Bilateral and multifocal retinal tumors
Presents early (average age 12 months)
High risk of osteosarcoma and soft-tissue sarcomas

right.title: Non-Heritable Retinoblastoma (60%)
points: Two acquired somatic mutations in a single retinal cell
Strictly unilateral and unifocal tumor
Presents later (average age 24 months)
No increased risk of secondary malignancies or inheritance

steps.tx: Development of bilateral ocular retinoblastoma combined with a midline intracranial pineal neuroblastic tumor defines a unique syndrome. Known as **trilateral retinoblastoma in children**, this rare clinical presentation occurs in patients with germline heritable RB1 mutations who develop a synchronous or metachronous pineoblastoma or suprasellar neuroblastic tumor, carrying a grave prognosis that warrants baseline brain magnetic resonance screening.
steps.say: Trilateral retinoblastoma occurs when bilateral retinoblastoma is accompanied by a midline pineoblastoma in children with germline RB1 mutations. Brain MRI screening is mandatory.

rows: Brain MRI at diagnosis and every 6 mos until age 5
Extremely rare manifestation of germline RB1
Early detection on asymptomatic MRI improves survival

steps.tx: Histopathological examination of enucleated specimens demonstrates distinctive neoplastic photoreceptor differentiation patterns. Microscopic examination displays small, round, hyperchromatic tumor cells with high nucleocytoplasmic ratios, forming classic **Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes in retinoblastoma**, comprising columnar cells encircling a central clear lumen representing primitive photoreceptor inner and outer segments, alongside Homer-Wright rosettes and fleurettes.
steps.say: Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes feature columnar cells encircling a central clear lumen, indicating photoreceptor differentiation. They are specific for retinoblastoma.

left.title: Flexner-Wintersteiner Rosettes
points: Specific pathognomonic hallmark of retinoblastoma
Columnar cells around central empty circular lumen
Represents early photoreceptor differentiation
Reflects favorable histological differentiation

right.title: Homer-Wright & Fleurettes
points: Homer-Wright: cells around tangled pink fibrillary neuropil
Seen in less differentiated areas of retinoblastoma
Fleurettes: bouquet-like clusters of photoreceptors
Reflects fully differentiated, benign-like retinoma

steps.tx: Under the microscope these tumour cells are caught remembering what they were meant to become. They line up around an empty central lumen in **Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes**, columnar cells mimicking the developing retina's photoreceptor layer, complete with the limiting membrane of a primitive eye. That architecture separates retinoblastoma from other small round cell tumours of childhood at a glance. Homer Wright rosettes nearby, wrapped around neuropil instead, borrow their pattern from neuroblastoma and remind the pathologist how primitive this family of tumours remains.
steps.say: Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes, cells ringing a clear lumen, show photoreceptor differentiation in retinoblastoma.

vis.alt: Microscopic histology of retinoblastoma showing Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes encircling central clear lumen
vis.caption: Microscopic histology of retinoblastoma showing Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes encircling central clear lumen. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Standardized classification frameworks categorize intraocular tumor extent and direct modern globe-salvaging therapeutic strategies. Utilizing the **International Classification for Intraocular Retinoblastoma** (ICIR), eyes are stratified from Group A (small tumors <=3 mm away from fovea and disc) to Group E (very advanced tumors with neovascular glaucoma, anterior chamber involvement, or phthisis bulbi), direct globe-preservation algorithms.
steps.say: The International Classification stratifies retinoblastoma from Group A small lesions to Group E advanced destroyed eyes. Groups A through C are managed with globe-salvaging therapies.

rows: Tumors <=3 mm, >3 mm from fovea & disc
Tumors >3 mm or macular, clear vitreous
Discrete focal subretinal or vitreous seeds
Diffuse subretinal fluid or diffuse vitreous seeds
Zero visual potential; high metastatic risk
Primary surgical enucleation with long optic nerve

steps.tx: Advanced targeted interventional chemotherapy modalities maximize globe preservation while minimizing systemic toxicities. First-line treatments for advanced intraocular disease utilize **superselective intra-arterial chemotherapy** (IAC), where a microcatheter is guided from the femoral artery directly into the ophthalmic artery to deliver concentrated melphalan, carboplatin, or topotecan, alongside intravitreal chemotherapy injections for refractory vitreous seeding.
steps.say: Intra-arterial chemotherapy delivers melphalan directly into the ophthalmic artery, dramatically improving eye preservation rates while avoiding systemic side effects.

left.title: Intra-Arterial Chemotherapy (IAC)
points: Cannulation of internal carotid and ophthalmic artery
Direct high-concentration infusion of melphalan
Preserves globes in up to 80% of Group D eyes
Avoids bone marrow suppression and systemic alopecia

right.title: Enucleation Indications
points: Group E eyes with intractable neovascular glaucoma
Optic nerve invasion or anterior chamber seeding
Blind, painful eye with phthisis bulbi
Must resect >=15 mm of retrobulbar optic nerve
